prompt: A pharmacy chain's head of operations reports 18,400 customers served last week; its marketing manager reports 15,900 for the same week. One counted till receipts, the other loyalty-card numbers. By lesson 1, what is the fix?
hint: Did either of them make a mistake?

choices.text: Ask the data team to find which of the two systems holds the error in its count
choices.why: Neither system is wrong: each counted something real. The two numbers answer two different definitions.

choices.text: Write one definition of a customer served and compute it in one place
choices.why: Right: this is Varanda's Monday problem again. Two unwritten definitions, cured by one written one, computed once.

choices.text: Report the average, 17,150, until the systems agree
choices.why: An average of two definitions measures neither of them, and the argument comes back next week.

choices.text: Buy a BI tool that connects both systems
choices.why: A tool draws whatever it is given. Connected to both systems, it would draw both numbers.

prompt: A logistics company launches a weekly report of deliveries per driver. Three months later the access log shows that only its author ever opens it. By lesson 1's cycle, where did the work go wrong?
hint: Which end of the loop is missing?

choices.text: It stopped at the answer
choices.why: Right: built, launched and visited by its author alone is the lesson's picture of stopping at the answer, with no decision and no action after it.

choices.text: The analysis chose its method before the question was understood
choices.why: Nothing says the method was wrong. The report may be accurate; nobody uses it.

choices.text: The data that was easy to get stood in for the data that mattered
choices.why: That failure gives a wrong answer to a real question. Here nobody is reading any answer at all.

choices.text: Deliveries per driver is not a BI question
choices.why: It can be: a recurring count answered the same way each week is exactly BI, if somebody decides with it.

prompt: Monday's total arrives R$ 1.4 million above an ordinary week, and nothing on the screen shows an error. By lesson 1, what has to be ruled out before it is sent?
hint: A number on a screen looks finished.

choices.text: A formula missing its $, which would give #DIV/0!
choices.why: That mistake announces itself with an error code, and there is none on the screen.

choices.text: Nothing, since a number with no error on the screen can be trusted
choices.why: Lesson 1 says the opposite: BI is not the truth by default, and the dangerous mistakes show no error.

choices.text: A function name typed in another language
choices.why: That gives #NAME?, an error anybody would see.

choices.text: A pipeline that ran twice and loaded the online orders twice
choices.why: Right: it is one of the lesson's examples of a number wrong with nothing on the screen saying so. Checking before publishing is part of the job.

prompt: In a spreadsheet set to English, an analyst types three stores' sales as 8840, 6460 and 7.040, the last copied from a Brazilian email meaning seven thousand and forty. What does =SUM(B2:B4) show?
hint: How does an English spreadsheet read the full stop?

choices.text: #VALUE!, because one cell holds text
choices.why: 7.040 is a valid number to an English spreadsheet, so there is nothing to refuse.

choices.text: 22340, because the sheet reads the format correctly
choices.why: That is the total the analyst meant. The spreadsheet does not know the email was Brazilian.

choices.text: 15307.04, a plausible total with no error
choices.why: Right: the full stop is read as a decimal point, so the third store counts as 7.04. Lesson 1 names this as one of the two mistakes that look fine.

choices.text: 15300, since the decimals are dropped
choices.why: SUM keeps decimals; nothing is dropped.

prompt: In lesson 1's cycle, what is measured after the action becomes the ___ at the start of the next lap.
hint: Where does every lap start?

prompt: Four requests reach the analyst of a supermarket chain in the same week. By lesson 2's test, which one most deserves an analysis?
hint: Options, a deadline, a cost of being wrong, and an answer that could change the choice.

choices.text: Which brand of paper bag to stock, a R$ 2,000-a-year choice that can be reversed next month
choices.why: The cost of being wrong is small and fixed next month, so an analysis costs more than it can save.

choices.text: Which of two sites to lease for a new store, signed for ten years in three weeks
choices.why: Right: two options, a deadline, a large cost of being wrong, and an answer that could move the choice.

choices.text: Absences by weekday, "to see", under a policy fixed by the union agreement
choices.why: This is Sônia's request again: no result could change anything, so the answer is worth nothing.

choices.text: Whether customers liked the new logo, which the board approved last week
choices.why: The decision has been taken. An analysis that arrives after it changes nothing, however good.

prompt: A restaurant franchise studies its 30 current restaurants, finds that every one in a shopping centre is profitable, and plans to open only in shopping centres. By lesson 2, what is missing from the data?
hint: Which restaurants have no row in this year's table?

choices.text: Those it opened there and later had to close
choices.why: Right: a closed restaurant leaves no row, so the survivors make shopping centres look safer than they were. That is survivorship.

choices.text: Each restaurant's sales per square metre
choices.why: A per-metre figure would still be computed only on the restaurants that are open today.

choices.text: A forecast of shopping-centre footfall for the next five years
choices.why: A forecast is about the future; the flaw here is in how the past was counted.

choices.text: The view of the franchise's most senior director
choices.why: That would add a HiPPO to the data, not the rows the data is missing.

prompt: A hotel's general manager is sure breakfast is what guests complain about most, having read three furious reviews last month. By lesson 2, what is the analyst's most useful first step?
hint: Memory keeps the vivid. What keeps the frequent?

choices.text: Agree, since experienced managers are right more often than not
choices.why: They often are, and the HiPPO's problem is that it carries the same weight on the days it is a guess.

choices.text: Ask the three reviewers for more detail
choices.why: More detail about three stays is still three stays: the sample the memory picked.

choices.text: Change the breakfast supplier at once, to show that guests are heard
choices.why: That acts on the anecdote before anybody has checked how often the complaint happens.

choices.text: Count complaints by subject over all stays for a long period
choices.why: Right: the records hold every stay counted the same way, which is the part of the picture memory cannot hold.

prompt: A chain has three shops. A sells R$ 5,400 thousand on 1,200 m², B R$ 7,200 thousand on 2,400 m², and C R$ 3,000 thousand on 1,000 m². Computed the way lesson 2 computes the chain's figure, what are its sales per square metre, in reais, to the nearest real?
hint: Total over total, not the average of the three shops' figures.

prompt: A bookshop chain's four shops, with their yearly sales and floor area. Put them in order of sales per square metre, highest first.
hint: Divide before you rank.
trap: Ranked by sales the order is exactly reversed: Leste sells the most and per square metre the least, as Contagem did at Varanda.

prompt: Four requests reach the data team of a gym chain. By lesson 3, which one is a data analyst's work?
hint: A question nobody has answered before, asked once.

choices.text: A monthly report of sign-ups by gym, counted as last year
choices.why: A recurring answer, the same way every time, is the BI analyst's.

choices.text: A nightly copy of the turnstile records into the database
choices.why: Data that arrives complete and on time is the data engineer's deliverable.

choices.text: Why sign-ups fell this January
choices.why: Right: a new question, explored once, answered with its evidence and its doubts.

choices.text: A score for each member's chance of cancelling next month
choices.why: A model that predicts case by case is the data scientist's.

prompt: Marketing's January sales exceed finance's by exactly the orders placed on 30 and 31 January and invoiced in February. By lesson 3, what should happen?
hint: Which of the three causes is this, and is either report wrong?

choices.text: Adjust marketing's report until it matches finance's total
choices.why: Making one report agree by adjusting it is exactly what the lesson rules out; the difference has a cause.

choices.text: Name it as two definitions, decide which is the company's and write it down
choices.why: Right: ordered against invoiced is the lesson's first cause. Both are right for their purpose; the company needs to say which one its sales figure uses.

choices.text: Let the data engineer choose, since both numbers pass through his pipelines
choices.why: The engineer moves data and should not decide what a sale is. That belongs to an owner.

choices.text: Average the two reports until the systems are aligned
choices.why: The systems are not misaligned; they count two moments. An average belongs to neither.

prompt: At an insurer, every dashboard computes "active policy" a little differently, each with its own formula. By lesson 3, which role is the company usually missing?
hint: Somebody who defines it once, in code, for every report.

choices.text: An analytics engineer
choices.why: Right: the lesson names this symptom — every dashboard computing a measure a little differently — as the sign of the missing role.

choices.text: A data analyst
choices.why: Exploring why the dashboards differ is useful once; it does not stop the next dashboard from differing again.

choices.text: A data scientist, to model which policies will lapse
choices.why: A model predicts; the problem here is a definition computed many ways.

choices.text: A data engineer to copy the data more often
choices.why: Fresher data computed five ways is still five numbers.

prompt: A gym chain reports "peak-hour attendance" every week. The operations director sets the staff rosters from it, an analyst computes it, and an engineer loads the turnstile data. By lesson 3, who should own its definition?
hint: For the repeat rate, the owner was Renata, not Lívia or Tiago.

choices.text: The engineer, since the data passes through his pipeline
choices.why: The engineer moves the data and should be told before a definition changes, not decide it.

choices.text: The analyst, since she computes it
choices.why: She keeps the written definition; the decision about what it means belongs to whoever acts on it.

choices.text: Whoever last changed the code
choices.why: That is what happens when nobody owns a number, and the lesson's point is that nobody then finds out.

choices.text: The operations director, who acts on it
choices.why: Right: the owner is the person who acts on the number and is told before it changes, with the analyst keeping the definition written.

prompt: A hospital is hiring for its data team. Match each line from its job adverts to the role it describes.
hint: Read the verbs, not the titles.

pairs.left: Keep the nightly load of admissions running and complete
Maintain the monthly occupancy report and its written definitions
Find out why emergency waits rose last winter
Build a model that scores each patient's risk of readmission

prompt: Taking a request, Lívia hears Caio say he will decide in June whether to add a second shift at the warehouse, and that he would add it if more than 15% of orders leave late two months running. Which of lesson 4's five questions does that last part answer?
hint: Which question names the result that would make him act?

choices.text: By when?
choices.why: June is the deadline; the 15% is something else.

choices.text: How is the number defined?
choices.why: That one asks what "late" counts and over what period; the threshold is the answer to another question.

choices.text: What would change your mind?
choices.why: Right: it names, before anybody sees the data, the result that would make him act, which is what makes the request measurable.

choices.text: Who decides?
choices.why: Caio decides, but the 15% is not about who; it is about which result would move him.

prompt: A hospital analyst publishes a weekly admissions report. By lesson 4's rule for checking before publishing, which check is worth her ten minutes?
hint: Against something independent, and able to catch a mistake you can name.

choices.text: Run the same query a second time and see it return the same total
choices.why: The same query on the same data repeats any mistake it made. It is a ritual, not a check.

choices.text: Compare the total with the admissions office's own count
choices.why: Right: an independent source, like Lívia's check against finance's daily takings. It would catch a missing ward or a double load.

choices.text: Make sure every chart has a title and a legend
choices.why: Useful for reading, but no title catches a wrong number.

choices.text: Ask the clinical director whether the number looks right
choices.why: That checks the number against an expectation, which is how wrong numbers that look right get through.

prompt: Another analyst logs 168 hours in a month: requests 30, meetings 24, checking and fixing data 40, recurring reports 20, definitions and notes 16, building dashboards 30, learning 8. Grouped as lesson 4 groups Lívia's log, what share went on making sure the numbers mean what they say?
hint: Two rows, as in Lívia's second sum.

choices.text: 33.3%: checking plus definitions
choices.why: Right: (40 + 16) ÷ 168 = 33.3%, the same grouping as Lívia's 29.5%.

choices.text: 32.1%, requests and meetings
choices.why: That is time with the people who ask the questions, the first of the two sums.

choices.text: 23.8%, checking and fixing data alone
choices.why: Lesson 4 adds definitions and notes to the checks; both are about what the numbers mean.

choices.text: 17.9%, the hours spent building dashboards
choices.why: Building is the visible part; the lesson's point is that the trust comes from the other hours.

prompt: Sônia asks Lívia for a report of staff costs for the board. Which version fits lesson 4's responsibilities?
hint: A report shows what its reader needs and no more.

choices.text: Every employee's salary by name, so the board sees the detail
choices.why: The board decides about totals and trends; names add nothing to that and expose everyone.

choices.text: Nothing, because salary data may never leave HR
choices.why: Lesson 4 does not forbid the report; it says how much detail it carries.

choices.text: Salaries by name, in a separate file sent only to Helena
choices.why: A smaller audience does not change what the report needs to show.

choices.text: Costs by department and salary band, with no names
choices.why: Right: salaries appear by band, not by name, and the reader gets what the decision needs.

prompt: After the fifteen-minute conversation, Lívia writes the request down in five lines and sends it back for Renata to ___, which stops the work drifting while it is being done.
hint: What does the person who asked do with the written version?

prompt: A company decides to skip descriptive reports and go straight to a vendor's forecasting model, "to work at the top of the staircase". By lesson 6, what is the risk?
hint: What does a forecast extend?

choices.text: Forecasting is the lower step of the staircase, so the company would be going backwards
choices.why: The staircase runs the other way, and lesson 6 rejects the staircase as the picture anyway.

choices.text: A forecast needs no history, so the descriptive work would be wasted
choices.why: A forecast extends a series somebody first counted; without the count there is nothing to extend.

choices.text: A forecast built on a miscounted year looks more authoritative than the miscount
choices.why: Right: every other kind stands on the description, and a wrong one carries into the forecast with more authority.

choices.text: None, as long as the vendor's model has a low error on its demo data
choices.why: A low error on somebody else's data says nothing about a company whose own year was never counted correctly.

prompt: A gym chain's analyst writes up March. Which sentence is a descriptive finding in lesson 6's sense?
hint: Period, comparison, what is known, and what is still open.

choices.text: March was weak, probably because of Carnival. Sign-ups are up overall.
choices.why: This is the weak version: a guess travelling with the authority of a count, and no comparison.

choices.text: March 2026: 1,840 sign-ups, 4.2% below March 2025, the year's only month below 2025. Cause not yet investigated.
choices.why: Right: a period, a comparison with the same month a year before, what stands out, and an honest line about what is still open.

choices.text: March fell 4.2% because Carnival moved into March this year.
choices.why: The cause may be right, but nobody has checked it; explaining is the diagnostic step, done separately.

choices.text: Sign-ups are strong and growing, especially downtown.
choices.why: No period, no number, no comparison: the reader supplies all three from memory.

prompt: A company has two stores. Store A sold 1,000 last year and 1,100 this year; store B sold 4,000 and 4,080. What did the company grow this year, computed the way lesson 6 computes the year's growth? In per cent, to one decimal.
hint: From the totals, not the average of 10% and 2%.

prompt: In a growth rate, new over old minus one, the old value is the ___, and it decides how large the percentage comes out.
hint: The part of a ratio below the line.

prompt: By lesson 6's arithmetic, which of these statements are correct? Choose all that apply.
hint: Work each one out before choosing.

choices.text: A share going from 8% to 10% rose 2 points, and 25%
choices.why: Right: 10 − 8 is 2 points; 10 ÷ 8 − 1 is 25%. Both are true and they are different numbers.

choices.text: Sales that rise 20% and then fall 20% end 4% below where they began
choices.why: Right: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96. The fall is 20% of a bigger base.

choices.text: Two years at 10% a year add up to 20% in total
choices.why: Growth compounds: 1.1 × 1.1 is 1.21, so 21%.

choices.text: An average of monthly growth rates gives the year's growth only when the months are the same size
choices.why: Right: the average gives each month one vote; the year weighs each month by its size.

choices.text: A month 26% above the month before was a good month
choices.why: At a seasonal business that may be the season alone; November 2025 was 26.1% above October and 2024 had a similar jump.

prompt: A bakery sold 400 cakes last May. This year's first half came to 2,150 against 2,000 in last year's. With the method that won lesson 8's backtest, what is the forecast for May?
hint: Last year's month times the recent growth.

choices.why: Right: 400 × 2,150 ÷ 2,000 = 430, last May times the first half's growth of 7.5%.
That is the seasonal naive forecast, which assumes no growth.
That is the first half spread evenly over six months, which ignores the season.
That adds 15%, twice the growth the two halves show.

prompt: Two methods are backtested on a pharmacy's sales. Method A has a MAPE of 3% and was below the actual in every month; method B has a MAPE of 4% with misses both ways. The forecast sets each month's stock order. By lesson 8, what is the bigger worry?
hint: Check the signs before the average.

choices.text: B, since a higher MAPE is always the worse method
choices.why: The size of the miss is one question; whether it leans one way is another, and here it decides.

choices.text: B, because errors in both directions mean it cannot be trusted
choices.why: Errors both ways largely cancel over a period; that is noise around the right level, not a missing ingredient.

choices.text: Neither, because both MAPEs are under 5%
choices.why: A MAPE means nothing on its own, and a small one with all errors on one side still empties shelves.

choices.text: A, whose misses all lean low, so stock runs short every month
choices.why: Right: that is bias, and it accumulates instead of cancelling. Like the seasonal naive method, A is missing an ingredient, probably growth.

prompt: A cinema forecasts that a film will sell few tickets, so it gives the film only two sessions a day. Ticket sales come in low, as forecast. By lesson 8, how can the forecast be checked?
hint: Find something the forecast could not have influenced.

choices.text: Compare the forecast with the tickets sold, day by day
choices.why: The tickets sold were shaped by the forecast itself, through the number of sessions, so they agree by construction.

choices.text: Run the forecast again with more history
choices.why: More history does not undo the effect the first forecast had on this film's sales.

choices.text: Check whether its sessions sold out
choices.why: Right: sold-out sessions are demand the data of sales cannot show, the cinema's version of the empty hose-reel shelf.

choices.text: Ask the manager whether the forecast felt right
choices.why: An opinion is not a measurement the forecast could not have influenced.

prompt: Varanda will open a store in Uberlândia in September 2026, and Otávio asks for its December forecast. By lesson 8, what is the honest way to make it?
hint: A method that copies last year's month needs a last year.

choices.text: Take the nine stores' average December and the backtest's 2.3% range
choices.why: The 2.3% was measured on stores with history; a new store's forecast carries a far wider miss.

choices.text: Borrow a similar store's shape and give a far wider range
choices.why: Right: the lesson's workaround, with the assumption stated and a range that says how little is known.

choices.text: Use the naive method, since it needs only last month
choices.why: The naive method ignores the season, and December is the season at its peak.

choices.text: Refuse, since a store with no history cannot be forecast
choices.why: The lesson says it is a guess dressed in a method, not useless; it gives a way to make it.

prompt: A method's backtest missed by about 2% a month for two years. In the last three months its errors were 9%, 11% and 10%, all too high. By lesson 8, what should the analyst do?
hint: What does a backtest that suddenly gets worse, in one direction, signal?

choices.text: Say the method has stopped working
choices.why: Right: errors that jump, all one way, are the sign of a break in the pattern; the past has stopped describing the future.

choices.text: Keep publishing it; three months is too short to judge
choices.why: Three misses five times the usual size, all one way, are not the noise the old range describes.

choices.text: Widen the range to 10% and carry on
choices.why: A wider range around a method that now leans one way still centres every forecast in the wrong place.

choices.text: Average the three months into the MAPE so it rises a little
choices.why: Blending a break into two years of good months hides it instead of reporting it.

prompt: A table sells for R$ 500 and costs R$ 300. Without a discount it is expected to sell 200 units. At 15% off, how many units must it sell to earn the same profit, counting price minus cost?
hint: The profit to match, divided by the margin per unit at the new price.

prompt: A product sells 30 units a day. Its reorder point was set at 240, for a 5-day lead time plus 3 safety days. The supplier now takes 8 days, and nobody changes the 240. How many units are on the shelf when an on-time delivery arrives?
hint: Eight days of sales come out of the 240 while the order travels.

choices.text: 90, three days of safety, as the rule was built to keep
choices.why: That was true at a 5-day lead time. The three extra days ate the cushion.

choices.text: 240, since the reorder point did not change
choices.why: The point is where an order is placed, not what is left when it arrives.

choices.text: 150, because 5 days of sales are taken from 240
choices.why: That uses the old lead time; the order now takes 8 days.

choices.text: None: the last unit leaves as the truck arrives
choices.why: Right: 240 − 30 × 8 = 0. The safety stock is gone, and any lateness is now an empty shelf, which no receipt will record.

prompt: Two analysts receive the same demand forecast for a product and recommend different order quantities. By lesson 9, what is the likeliest reason, and is one of them wrong?
hint: The forecast is an input. What else goes into a prescriptive question?

choices.text: One of them misread the forecast, so one is wrong
choices.why: Possible, but the lesson's point is that the same forecast honestly leads to different answers.

choices.text: One used a solver and the other a spreadsheet
choices.why: The size of the tool does not change the shape; given the same objective, both should agree.

choices.text: They weigh the two costs of stock differently
choices.why: Right: the forecast is an input and the objective is a choice. Weighing the two is a business decision for whoever owns it.

choices.text: Prescriptive answers are random, so both are wrong
choices.why: Nothing random is involved; each answer follows from a stated objective.

prompt: A product costs R$ 60. Four options for next month, with their estimated units. Put them in order of profit (price minus cost, times units), highest first.
hint: Compute each margin first: 40, 35, 30 and 20.
trap: By sales the order is reversed, 20% off first. Profit is 40,000, 38,500, 37,500 and 36,000: each discount gives away margin that the extra units do not win back.

prompt: Caio wants one number to tell him, every quarter, whether the warehouse's automatic reorder rules are working. By lesson 9, which one?
hint: The outcome that says a rule failed.

choices.text: The number of purchase orders the rules raised
choices.why: That measures how busy the rules were, not whether the shelves had stock.

choices.text: Days each product was out of stock
choices.why: Right: the lesson names it as the number that says the rule failed, and it is the one the sales data cannot show by itself.

choices.text: The products' sales for the quarter
choices.why: A sale that never happened leaves no receipt, so sales cannot show the cost of an empty shelf.

choices.text: The average lead time across suppliers
choices.why: An input to the rule, worth owning, but not the outcome that tells whether it worked.

prompt: A furniture shop's week: 40 orders delivered, 34 of them by the promised day; 3 orders cancelled before their promised day; 2 cancelled after it had passed. With the definition on lesson 10's card, what is the week's rate, in per cent to one decimal?
hint: Which cancellations join the denominator?

prompt: An online shop has 200,000 visits a month, converts 2% and has an average ticket of R$ 150. A campaign raises visits by 20%, conversion falls to 1.8%, and the ticket holds. By lesson 10's tree, what happens to sales?
hint: The parts of a product move the result in proportion: 1.2 × 0.9.

choices.text: They rise 8%, to R$ 648 thousand
choices.why: Right: 240,000 × 1.8% × 150 = 648,000 against 600,000. A branch is only good news as far as the others let it be.

choices.text: They are unchanged
choices.why: That was Renata's case, where visits rose 25% and conversion fell a fifth. Here the numbers differ.

choices.text: They rise 20%, following the visits
choices.why: Only if the other branches held still; conversion fell by a tenth.

choices.text: They fall 10%, following conversion
choices.why: Conversion is one branch of three; visits rose more than it fell.

prompt: A hospital's KPI card for "beds cleaned within two hours of discharge" names its owner as "Housekeeping". What does lesson 10 say about that?
hint: Who can be asked on Monday why the number fell?

choices.text: Fine: the department that does the cleaning owns it
choices.why: A department cannot be asked why the number fell; a person can.

choices.text: A KPI that crosses departments should have no owner
choices.why: Without an owner it is a metric again: nobody is expected to act when it moves.

choices.text: The analyst who computes it should be named instead
choices.why: The analyst computes it; the owner explains it and acts.

choices.text: One named person, who explains it and decides
choices.why: Right: the owner is one person, never a department, and need not cause every movement in it.

prompt: A KPI's last twelve weeks ran between 60% and 70%, with a median of 65%, and nothing changed in that time. By lesson 10, which goal and action threshold belong on its card?
hint: Above the best week; just under the worst, and not for one week only.

choices.text: Goal 66%; act below 64%
choices.why: A goal met by luck in half the weeks and an alarm inside the normal range, ringing all the time.

choices.text: Goal 95%; act below 50%
choices.why: A goal nobody could reach is a wish, and a threshold far below anything seen never fires.

choices.text: Goal 75% by year end; act below 59% two weeks running
choices.why: Right: the goal needs something to change, and the threshold sits just under the worst week, so it fires on a real problem.

choices.text: Goal 70%; act after any single week that falls below 65%
choices.why: 70% has already been reached, and half the weeks fall below 65% with nothing wrong.

prompt: By lesson 10, how often a KPI is read follows the ___ it feeds, not how often its data refreshes.
hint: Caio's data refreshes hourly and his card says weekly.

prompt: A bank's complaints team is now rewarded on "average days to close a complaint". By lesson 11, which guard belongs beside it?
hint: What is the cheapest way to close a complaint fast without solving it?

choices.text: The number of complaints received each month
choices.why: That moves with the bank's service, not with how the team closes complaints.

choices.text: The share of complaints reopened by the same customer
choices.why: Right: closing before the problem is solved is the shortcut, and a reopened complaint is what it leaves behind, like the call centre's repeat calls.

choices.text: The same average, reported twice a week instead of weekly
choices.why: Reading the KPI more often does not show how it was moved.

choices.text: The team's overtime hours
choices.why: Overtime might rise or fall either way; it does not reveal complaints closed unsolved.

prompt: A hospital asks its analyst for one page of 18 indicators to serve the board, the ward managers and the pharmacy together. By lesson 11, what should she propose?
hint: The working limit is per what?

choices.text: A handful per audience, the rest kept as metrics
choices.why: Right: five to seven per audience, and the indicators that miss a page are not deleted; they stay available.

choices.text: Cut to the 6 the board prefers and send that page to everybody
choices.why: Six chosen for the board serve the board. The pharmacy acts on different numbers.

choices.text: Keep the 18, sorted so the most important are at the top
choices.why: A reader cannot ignore numbers selectively; eighteen on one page are read shallowly or skipped.

choices.text: Average the 18 into one hospital score
choices.why: A score nobody can trace back to a cause gives no one anything to act on.

prompt: At the quarterly review, Helena announces that the operations objective for next year moves from keeping the delivery date to cutting delivery cost. By lesson 11's routine, what happens to Caio's page?
hint: The method starts from the objective.

choices.text: Nothing until an indicator has gone two reviews without action
choices.why: That rule retires one indicator; a changed objective changes the questions the whole page answers.

choices.text: Delivery cost per order is added as a sixth indicator
choices.why: One in, one out: the page keeps its size, and the cut comes from a new scoring rather than an addition.

choices.text: Each director votes on which indicators stay
choices.why: A vote is the contest of seniority the written reasons exist to avoid.

choices.text: Redo the scoring with the new questions; the page follows
choices.why: Right: the second question of the review. Delivery cost per order, parked at 38 points, is likely to score differently now.

prompt: By lesson 11's question — what is the cheapest way to move this number without improving what it stands for? — match each KPI to its guard.
hint: Find the shortcut first, then what it damages.

pairs.left: New contracts signed by the sales team
Items picked per hour in the warehouse
Patients seen per hour at a clinic
pairs.right: Patients back within 7 days with the same complaint

prompt: Reading time is the visible cost of an indicator. Which of these does lesson 11 name as the costs paid out of sight? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three, each paid by somebody every week.

choices.text: Extracting the data and checking it every week
choices.why: Right: somebody has to notice when the source changes.

choices.text: Keeping its card true as things change
choices.why: Right: an indicator whose card has drifted gives a number nobody can explain.

choices.text: A licence fee per indicator in the BI tool
choices.why: Tools are not priced per indicator, and the lesson's costs are work and attention.

choices.text: The attention of the owner who must act on it
choices.why: Right: on forty, the owner acts on whichever was mentioned last.

choices.text: Choosing a colour for its chart
choices.why: That costs a minute once, and the lesson does not count it.

prompt: Store X delivered 60 of 100 furniture orders and 270 of 300 parcels on time, 82.5% overall. Store Y delivered 260 of 400 furniture orders and 95 of 100 parcels on time, 71% overall. Compared on a half-and-half mix, as lesson 12 does, what is store Y's rate, in per cent?
hint: Each kind's rate first, then their simple average.

prompt: A software company's help desk reports "tickets up 25%": 400 last quarter, 500 this quarter. Active users went from 10,000 to 15,000. By lesson 12, what is the honest reading?
hint: Out of how many chances?

choices.text: Support got worse: tickets rose 25%
choices.why: A count with no denominator says how much, not how often; the base grew faster.

choices.text: Per hundred users, tickets rose, because users grew faster than tickets
choices.why: Users growing faster than tickets makes the rate fall, not rise.

choices.text: Per hundred users, tickets fell from 4.0 to 3.3
choices.why: Right: 400 ÷ 10,000 and 500 ÷ 15,000. Each user was less likely to need help.

choices.text: Nothing can be said without a full year
choices.why: Two quarters with their bases are enough to compute both rates.

prompt: An estate agency sold 12 flats last month: ten between R$ 300 and 500 thousand, and two penthouses at R$ 6 million each. A buyer asks what a typical flat sold for. By lesson 12, which number answers the buyer?
hint: A question about money, or about people?

choices.text: The mean of all twelve, since it uses every sale
choices.why: The two penthouses drag the mean to well over R$ 1 million, where no flat in the ten sits.

choices.text: The median of the twelve
choices.why: Right: a typical buyer is a question about people, and the median stays among them.

choices.text: The highest price, which shows what the market can reach
choices.why: That answers a question nobody asked and describes one sale.

choices.text: The total divided by eleven, leaving the dearest penthouse out
choices.why: One penthouse is still in, so the figure still sits above every ordinary flat.

prompt: A lender's default rate went from 2% to 3% in a year. Which sentence is right?
hint: A difference between two percentages, and a relative change.

choices.text: It rose 1 percentage point, which is a 50% rise
choices.why: Right: points for the difference, per cent for the relative change, and both given when it matters.

choices.text: It rose 1%
choices.why: 1 is the difference in points; written as per cent it understates a 50% rise.

choices.text: It rose 50 percentage points
choices.why: 50 is the relative change, in per cent; in points it moved one.

choices.text: It rose 1 percentage point, which is the same as saying 1%
choices.why: Points and per cent are different measures; here one says 1 and the other 50.

prompt: A fitness app reports to its board. Which of these are vanity metrics when shown as progress? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which ones cannot fall?

choices.text: App downloads since launch
choices.why: Right: a cumulative total, a record every quarter by construction.

choices.text: Members who logged a workout in the last 30 days
choices.why: This can fall, which is what makes it worth reading.

choices.text: Workouts logged since launch
choices.why: Right: it counts everybody who ever trained and nobody who stopped.

choices.text: Registered accounts
choices.why: Right: nobody deletes an account when they stop, as with Varanda's registered customers.

choices.text: Subscriptions renewed this month
choices.why: A bad month shows here at once; a team could act on it.

prompt: A hospital builds a bed-occupancy dashboard. The head of nursing will set her staff rosters from it, but she cannot approve or stop the project. Where does lesson 13's map put her?
hint: Low power, high interest.

choices.text: Manage closely
choices.why: That quadrant is for people who can shape or stop the project.

choices.text: Keep satisfied
choices.why: That is high power and low interest, the reverse of her position.

choices.text: Monitor
choices.why: Her interest is high: her rosters depend on it.

choices.text: Keep informed
choices.why: Right: she will live with it every day. Tell her what is coming, ask what she needs, show her the mock.

prompt: Caio asks that Helena's monthly line on the delivery KPI also show each region's rate, "so she has the full picture". What does lesson 13 say?
hint: What decision does Helena make with it, and what would a breakdown invite?

choices.text: Give her the same page as Caio, with a filter
choices.why: One page with filters for everybody is the mistake the lesson starts from.

choices.text: Add it, since the CEO should see every level of detail
choices.why: More detail is not more use; her question is whether the promise is being kept.

choices.text: One number and its trend; regions one click below
choices.why: Right: a breakdown by region invites her to manage regions, which is Caio's job.

choices.text: Show regions to Helena and drop the company figure
choices.why: That removes the one number her decision rests on.

prompt: In his interview, Marcos says that today he phones each driver at ten to find out who is behind. Which interview question did that answer, and what does the answer give the project?
hint: There is always an answer, often a phone call.

choices.text: "What would make you act differently?" — his threshold
choices.why: A threshold is a number at which he acts; a ten o'clock round of calls is how he finds out.

choices.text: "How do you know today?" — the bar to beat
choices.why: Right: the current way of knowing is the benchmark; a board slower or less precise than the calls is no use to him.

choices.text: "Who else should I talk to?" — the drivers
choices.why: He named the drivers' team leaders for that question, not the calls.

choices.text: "Tell me about the last time" — a recent case
choices.why: A last-time story is one decision told in detail; this is his routine way of knowing.

prompt: A clinic builds a dashboard of missed appointments. Match each person to the way lesson 13 says they have a stake.
hint: Decides, influences, is affected, provides the data.

pairs.left: The clinic's director, who approves the budget
The finance manager, whose view the director listens to
The receptionists, who will call patients from it each morning
The technician who exports the booking system each night

prompt: Put lesson 13's interview questions in the order Lívia asks them.
hint: From the work itself to the people who are missing.
items: What decisions do you make about deliveries, and how often?
Tell me about the last time you made one.
What would make you act differently?
How do you know today, without the dashboard?
Who else should I talk to?
trap: Asking about thresholds before the person has described a real decision gets a number from nowhere; the recent case is what grounds it.

prompt: A supermarket's bakery manager restocks the bread shelves every two hours from a board whose data is copied every 30 minutes. A vendor offers a real-time feed at three times the cost. By lesson 14, is it worth it?
hint: What sets how fresh is fresh enough?

choices.text: No: he acts every two hours
choices.why: Right: the rhythm of the decision sets the freshness. A newer picture would change nothing he does.

choices.text: Yes: newer data is always worth more to an operational decision
choices.why: Only if somebody would act differently because of it; he acts every two hours.

choices.text: Yes, because a board without real time cannot show exceptions
choices.why: Exceptions come from how the board is laid out, not from the speed of the copy.

choices.text: No, because bread is a tactical decision, read monthly
choices.why: Restocking a shelf every two hours is operational; the reason is the rhythm, not the level.

prompt: A board's data is copied every 15 minutes. By the reasoning behind Marcos's 20-minute rule, when should the board hide its numbers and show a warning instead?
hint: One missed copy is a hiccup.

choices.text: After 15 minutes, as soon as one copy is late
choices.why: One missed copy can be a hiccup, and hiding the board for every hiccup teaches people to ignore the warning.

choices.text: Never: grey the old numbers and add a small note
choices.why: Grey numbers with a small warning are still read as current from a loading bay.

choices.text: After 20 minutes, the number Marcos uses
choices.why: The 20 was derived from a 10-minute copy; with copies every 15 it would fire between two normal copies.

choices.text: After about 30 minutes, two missed copies
choices.why: Right: twenty was twice a ten-minute interval; here twice fifteen is thirty.

prompt: One morning Marcos's board announces 572 orders for the day, on a plan of 286. By lesson 14, how should the number be treated?
hint: Exactly twice the plan.

choices.text: As a record day: call in extra vans
choices.why: Acting on it sends vans for orders that do not exist; the board is acted on before anybody checks.

choices.text: As normal variation, since daily orders move a lot
choices.why: Exactly double the plan is not variation; it is the shape of a duplicated load.

choices.text: As a data problem until shown otherwise
choices.why: Right: a total that jumps against the plan is checked against what was expected, and the board says so.

choices.text: As a reason to raise the alert threshold
choices.why: The threshold is about minutes behind; this is a count that is wrong.

prompt: Which message from a call centre's operational board is an alert in lesson 14's sense?
hint: Who should do what, now, with the data to do it.

choices.text: The queue is long.
choices.why: A fact with no person, no action and no size.

choices.text: Line B: 14 waiting, longest 11 min; Ana's team has 4 free: move 2 to line B?
choices.why: Right: it names where, how bad, who can help and the action, like the route 11 message.

choices.text: Average wait today: 3 min 40 s, above the 3-minute target.
choices.why: An average across the day says nothing about which line needs help now.

choices.text: Calls are waiting in the queue. Please check the board when you have a moment and act as needed.
choices.why: It hands the person a chore, not an action, and no data to take one.

prompt: Bruno asks for a screen on the Contagem store floor, read by the staff between customers. By lesson 14, which of these belong on it? Choose all that apply.
hint: What needs attention now, and how old the data is.

choices.text: The time the data describes, and its age
choices.why: Right: without it, a frozen screen looks calm.

choices.text: Best sellers missing from the shelf right now
choices.why: Right: an exception somebody on the floor can act on in minutes.

choices.text: This year's monthly sales against last year's, as two lines
choices.why: That answers a tactical question and changes nothing before lunch.

choices.text: Customer pick-up orders already past their promised time
choices.why: Right: counted customers waiting, first in the list.

choices.text: The nine stores ranked by sales per square metre
choices.why: A ranking over a year is strategic or tactical, not something the floor acts on today.

prompt: Caio's review discusses a variance only when it is more than R$ 5 thousand and more than 10% of its line, as Renata's does. Four cost lines this month: A +R$ 3 thousand (+25%), B +R$ 12 thousand (+6%), C −R$ 9 thousand (−15%), D +R$ 6 thousand (+8%). Which ones are discussed?
hint: Both conditions, and the sign does not matter for this rule.

choices.text: Only C
choices.why: Right: it is the one above both bars. Being favourable does not exempt it: the review still asks whether it is timing or real.

choices.text: B, C and D, all above R$ 5 thousand
choices.why: B and D are under 10% of their lines.

choices.text: A and C, the two largest percentages
choices.why: A is R$ 3 thousand: a large percentage of a small line.

choices.text: Only B, the largest amount
choices.why: B is large in reais and small against its line, 6%.

prompt: On 2 December, Sônia wants to review November's overtime from the timesheet system, three days before payroll closes the month. By lesson 15, what should the review use?
hint: Which figures does a monthly review use?

choices.text: The timesheet count now, since it is the most recent
choices.why: Corrections and late entries land after the 2nd; the meeting would argue with the payroll figure for its first twenty minutes.

choices.text: The budget for November, until the actual is known
choices.why: The budget is what the actual is compared with, not a stand-in for it.

choices.text: An average of the timesheet count and October's close
choices.why: Mixing two months and two sources gives a number belonging to neither.

choices.text: The closed figures, as finance reports them
choices.why: Right: tactical data waits for the month to close, which is a decision about definitions as much as timing.

prompt: A garden centre expects about 30% of May's sales on the Mother's Day weekend, the second Sunday of the month. On 15 May its weekly check compares sales so far with half of May's target. By lesson 15, what is wrong?
hint: Does the target arrive evenly?

choices.text: Nothing: half the month should bring half the target
choices.why: Only if sales were even across the month, and here a big weekend falls in the first half.

choices.text: Weekly checks are operational and do not belong in a monthly review
choices.why: The lesson keeps the weekly check; the problem is the yardstick it compares against.

choices.text: The share due by the 15th must follow the month's shape
choices.why: Right: against half the target the check reports a triumph now and a collapse later, with nothing changing in between.

choices.text: It should compare with last May's total instead
choices.why: A month's total is known only at the end; the check needs the part due by now.

prompt: Email brought orders at R$ 9.7 each in November, the cheapest channel by far. Renata proposes tripling the number of emails sent in December. By lesson 15, how should the action be written?
hint: R$ 9.7 is an average over the sends already made.

choices.text: As a transfer: triple it, since R$ 9.7 is under target
choices.why: The next sends reach people less ready to buy, and nobody knows what their orders will cost.

choices.text: As a test, with an owner and a date
choices.why: Right: like the R$ 15 thousand moved into paid search, the extra spend buys what was not worth buying before, so it is measured.

choices.text: Not at all: email is too small a line to discuss
choices.why: The line is small; tripling it is a decision with a cost, and the review is where it is set.

choices.text: As a finding, to be read aloud next month
choices.why: Reading numbers aloud decides nothing; an action needs an owner, a date and a measure.

prompt: Content production came in under budget because a photo shoot slipped into December. By lesson 15 that is a ___ variance: it moves between months, while a real one does not come back.
hint: A question of when the money is spent, not whether.

prompt: A company sold R$ 50 million in 2020 and R$ 70 million in 2024. A price index was 100 in 2020 and 125 in 2024. What is its compound annual growth rate in real terms over the period, in per cent to one decimal?
hint: Deflate 2024 first; then count the steps between the years.

prompt: A board pack computes the CAGR of sales from 2019 to 2025 with ^(1/7). By lesson 16, what is wrong, and which way does it err?
hint: Count the years of figures, then the steps between them.

choices.text: It should be ^(1/6), and the rate comes out too low
choices.why: Right: spreading the same total growth over one step too many understates each year, as the 6.2% did against 7.9%.

choices.text: Nothing: seven years of figures need the seventh root
choices.why: Seven figures hold six steps of growth, as five figures held four at Varanda.

choices.text: It should be ^(1/6), and the rate comes out too high
choices.why: A larger root spreads the growth thinner, which lowers the rate.

choices.text: It should be ^(1/8), counting both ends
choices.why: Counting both ends adds steps that never happened.

prompt: Varanda's board added staff training hours to its page as the learning-and-growth row. Two years on, training hours have risen and turnover, stock-outs and repeat customers have not moved. By lesson 16, what should the board be told?
hint: The scorecard is a hypothesis about how the company makes money.

choices.text: That it needs more time: leading indicators always take longer
choices.why: Two years with nothing moving above it is the evidence the chain was asked to produce.

choices.text: That the scorecard should be replaced by one north star metric
choices.why: One number is the all-money problem in a smaller size; the finding is about one arrow.

choices.text: That training is working, since its own number rose
choices.why: A leading row earns its place by moving the rows above it, not by rising itself.

choices.text: That the chain does not hold here, so the row is reconsidered
choices.why: Right: a hypothesis can be wrong, and the board should know rather than keep the row out of loyalty.

prompt: Lívia makes sure each number in the board pack is defined in 2025 as it was in 2021, because by lesson 16 a long run of figures whose definition changed midway is two ___ with one line drawn through them.
hint: What is a sequence of values over time called?

prompt: Hospital Jacarandá's board wants one measure per perspective of the balanced scorecard. Match each perspective to the measure that belongs in it.
hint: Owners, customers, what the hospital must be excellent at, and whether it can keep improving.

pairs.right: Share of patients who would recommend the hospital
Median wait in the emergency department

prompt: A card issuer processed 1,000,000 payments in a month, and 0.05% of them were fraud. Its rule flagged 400 of the frauds and 1% of the good payments. What is the rule's precision, in per cent to one decimal?
hint: First the frauds and the good payments; then right alerts over all alerts.

prompt: An analyst joins a car insurer and learns that many accidents are reported as claims only months after they happen. Which of lesson 17's four questions has she just answered?
hint: Where the records come from, and their habit.

choices.text: The decisions made over and over
choices.why: That question is about what the insurer decides, such as pricing a policy; this is about its records.

choices.text: The indicators that serve them
choices.why: No indicator has been named; she has learnt how the data arrives.

choices.text: Where the data comes from and what is odd about it
choices.why: Right: outcomes arriving late is a habit of the data, like a loan's default or a disputed card payment at Ipê.

choices.text: The typical trap
choices.why: The trap follows from this habit, for example a recent month that looks safe, but the habit itself is the third question.

prompt: Lender X had operating costs of R$ 50 million and total income of R$ 125 million; lender Y had R$ 90 million and R$ 300 million. By lesson 17's efficiency ratio, which runs more efficiently?
hint: Cost over income; lower is better.

choices.text: X, since its costs are lower in reais
choices.why: Costs mean little without the income they produce; the ratio puts them together.

choices.text: Y, at 30%, against X's 40%
choices.why: Right: Y spends R$ 30 to earn R$ 100 of income, X spends R$ 40.

choices.text: X, at 40%, because a higher ratio is better
choices.why: Lower is better, which surprises people the first time.

choices.text: Neither can be judged without the default rate
choices.why: Credit losses matter for profit, but the efficiency ratio answers its own question with these two numbers.

prompt: Put the lines of a lender's income statement in lesson 17's order, from the top to the profit.
hint: A chain of subtractions, with fees added once.
items: Minus funding cost, giving net interest income
Plus fee income, giving total income
Minus operating costs, giving profit before tax
trap: Taking operating costs out before credit losses gives the same profit and hides the line that grew 64.4% at Ipê; the lesson's chain keeps the cost of risk where the reader meets it first.

prompt: Ipê's rule A lets 100 frauds through and blocks 7,992 good payments a month; rule B lets 160 through and blocks 3,996. A fraud costs R$ 1,100. If a blocked good payment cost R$ 30 to handle instead of R$ 15, which rule would be cheaper?
hint: Missed frauds × 1,100 plus blocked good payments × 30, for each.

choices.text: Rule B, by about R$ 54 thousand a month
choices.why: Right: A costs 110,000 + 239,760 = 349,760; B costs 176,000 + 119,880 = 295,880. The threshold is a decision about the price of each mistake.

choices.text: Rule A, still, by about R$ 6 thousand
choices.why: That was the result at R$ 15. Doubling the price of a blocked customer moves it.

choices.text: Neither: both now cost more than having no rule
choices.why: No rule lets all 400 frauds through, R$ 440,000; both rules are below that.

choices.text: The one with the higher precision, whatever the prices
choices.why: Precision alone does not choose between rules, because the two mistakes cost different amounts.

prompt: An email campaign goes to 20,000 customers, who place 900 orders; a random holdout of 2,000 places 60. Every order used a 10% coupon on an average ticket of R$ 300, and sending cost R$ 3,000. What did each order the campaign caused cost, in reais?
hint: Incremental orders first: the difference in rates times 20,000. Then the whole cost over them.

prompt: A pharmacy chain's sales grew 12% last year. Two of its stores opened in the middle of the year before, and its like-for-like growth was 2%. The board asks whether the existing stores are selling better. What answers it?
hint: Which stores traded for the whole of both periods?

choices.text: The 12%, since it counts every store
choices.why: Counting every store is the problem: two of them had a half year in the base.

choices.text: The new stores' growth, which shows the trend
choices.why: Their growth compares a full year with half a year, like Ipatinga's 110.1%.

choices.text: The average of the two, 7%
choices.why: An average of two different questions answers neither.

choices.text: The 2%: the stores open for both whole years
choices.why: Right: the rest of the 12% is new stores' first full year, which says nothing about selling better.

prompt: In a 30-day month, a desk lamp sold 60 units in the 20 days it was on the shelf and was out of stock for the other 10. Estimated as lesson 18 does, how many sales did the empty shelf lose?
hint: The daily rate is over the days there was something to sell.

choices.text: About 20, at 2 a day over 30 days
choices.why: Dividing by 30 hides the empty days inside a lower average.

choices.text: None: the receipts show no lost sales
choices.why: The receipts cannot show it; a sale that did not happen leaves no record.

choices.text: About 30, at 3 a day
choices.why: Right: 60 ÷ 20 = 3 a day while it was there. The estimate leans one way and the other, and is still better than the receipts' zero.

choices.text: 60, the month's sales again
choices.why: That would assume the empty third of the month sold as much as the full two thirds.

prompt: A supplier sent ten orders in a quarter, every one complete, and six of them late. Its slide shows a fill rate of 100%. What should Caio take to the supplier meeting?
hint: Which measure looks at dates?

choices.text: The 100% fill rate, which is the supplier's own figure
choices.why: Fill rate counts units and ignores dates, so six late orders do not touch it.

choices.text: An OTIF of 40%, with the late orders
choices.why: Right: four of ten orders were complete and on time. A supplier reports the first number; a retailer measures the second.

choices.text: Nothing: a supplier that sends everything is reliable
choices.why: A complete order nine days late emptied the hose-reel hook.

choices.text: The average delay, since an average is fairer than counting orders
choices.why: An average delay of a couple of days is what nobody chases; the shelf emptied on the one long one.

prompt: Planning the next campaign, Renata proposes holding out the customers who live outside Belo Horizonte, "since deliveries there are slow and they buy less anyway". By lesson 18, what is wrong with that holdout?
hint: How must a holdout be chosen?

choices.text: It buys less for reasons of its own
choices.why: Right: a holdout must be drawn at random, so that the only difference between the groups is the campaign.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as it is about 10% of the list
choices.why: The share is fine; how the people were picked is not.

choices.text: It is too large to leave without the coupon
choices.why: Size is not the problem; Varanda held out 10% before.

choices.text: Customers outside the city cannot be tracked online
choices.why: They order online like anyone else; their orders are counted the same way.

prompt: Ten patients at another emergency department waited 22, 95, 15, 40, 180, 33, 61, 28, 120 and 47 minutes. A target reads "nine in ten seen within two hours". Which figure tests it?
hint: Sort them first.

choices.text: 64.1 minutes, the mean of the ten waits
choices.why: The mean answers a different question and is pulled up by the two long waits.

choices.text: 43.5 minutes, the median of the ten
choices.why: The median is the typical wait; the target is about the long end.

choices.text: 180 minutes, the longest wait
choices.why: The longest is the tenth; the target allows one in ten above the line.

choices.text: 120 minutes, the ninth in order
choices.why: Right: nine of ten were seen within 120 minutes, the 90th percentile, so the target is just met.

prompt: Two wards of the same size: a maternity ward where most deliveries are booked weeks ahead, and an emergency medical ward whose admissions vary from day to day. By lesson 19, which can safely run at the higher occupancy?
hint: What makes a full night common?

choices.text: Both should aim at 100%, so no bed is wasted
choices.why: A full ward leaves the next emergency nowhere to go.

choices.text: The emergency ward, because emergencies are more urgent
choices.why: Urgent and unpredictable is the reason it needs more spare room, not less.

choices.text: The first one: its demand is planned and steady
choices.why: Right: the right ceiling depends on how variable admissions are, and booked deliveries vary less.

choices.text: Both should run at the same 85%, whatever their patients
choices.why: 85% is a working rule for general beds, and the lesson says the level depends on the ward.

prompt: Jacarandá reports a 30-day readmission rate of 6.5%; a hospital across town reports 8.5%. By lesson 19, what has to be checked before saying Jacarandá does better?
hint: There are at least three defensible denominators.

choices.text: Which hospital has more beds
choices.why: Size does not explain a rate; the definition behind it can.

choices.text: How each one defines it
choices.why: Right: Jacarandá's own October was 8.5% on one definition and 6.5% on another, so the gap may be two definitions rather than two hospitals.

choices.text: Nothing: 6.5% is lower, so it is better
choices.why: Lower only means better when both are counted the same way.

choices.text: Whether the other hospital uses a dashboard
choices.why: The tool does not change the rate; the denominator does.

prompt: Town A has a higher crude rate of heart-failure admissions than town B and a lower age-adjusted one. Jacarandá is planning how many cardiology beds to keep for next year's patients from town A. By lesson 19, which rate serves that decision?
hint: Beds are filled by actual patients, of whatever age.

choices.text: The crude rate, because A really sends more patients
choices.why: Right: the crude rate says how much illness a town has; the adjusted one says whether its people are likelier to fall ill at the same age.

choices.text: The age-adjusted rate, because it is the fair comparison
choices.why: Fair between towns, but a bed planner needs how much illness A actually has, not what it would have at another age mix.

choices.text: Neither: counts, because rates hide the patients
choices.why: For one town and one hospital the count and the crude rate point the same way; it is the age adjustment that does not fit this question.

choices.text: An average of the crude and adjusted rates
choices.why: The two answer different questions; averaging them answers none.

prompt: Four wards of another hospital in a 30-day month, with their beds and patient-days. Put them in order of bed occupancy, highest first.
hint: Patient-days over beds × 30.
trap: By patient-days the order is ward 2, 3, 1, 4; occupancy divides by the beds available: 95%, 90%, 80% and 70%.

prompt: Another machine's shift: 480 minutes, a 40-minute planned break, 40 minutes of unplanned stops, an ideal cycle of 20 seconds, 1,050 parts made and 1,000 good. What is its OEE, in per cent to one decimal?
hint: The short route: ideal time for the good parts over the planned time.

prompt: Over 2,000 running hours, machine P failed 40 times and was repaired in an hour each time; machine Q failed 4 times, 10 hours each. Both come out at an availability of 98.0%. By lesson 20, what does the report need beside it?
hint: How often, and how long.

choices.text: Nothing: equal availability means equal machines
choices.why: One number hides two very different patterns of failure, as IM-07 against IM-11 did.

choices.text: Their MTTR alone, since Q's ten-hour repairs are the problem
choices.why: Q's long repairs are visible already; P's forty failures are what the single number hides.

choices.text: Only the OEE of each machine
choices.why: OEE folds stops into availability again; the frequency still disappears.

choices.text: MTBF: P stops every 50 hours, Q every 500
choices.why: Right: forty quick repairs are usually one small fault fixed again and again, and each restart costs warm-up and scrap the repair time does not show.

prompt: A control chart for another machine has limits of 1.0% and 4.0%, computed from a stable month. This week's scrap rates were 2.1, 3.8, 2.6, 4.3 and 3.0%. By lesson 20, which day is worth looking for a cause?
hint: A signal is a value outside the limits.

choices.text: The 3.8% day, close to the limit
choices.why: Inside the limits is what the process does sometimes; adjusting for it adds variation.

choices.text: Every day above the 2.5% centre of the limits
choices.why: Half of all ordinary days fall above the centre; that is the wrong reaction the chart prevents.

choices.text: The 4.3% day, above the upper limit
choices.why: Right: a value ordinary variation would very rarely produce, like day 9 and its new lot of resin.

choices.text: None, since the week's average of 3.2% is inside the limits
choices.why: The chart is read point by point; an average would bury the one signal.

prompt: A customer's contract limits defects to 100 ppm. This quarter it received 400,000 of Serra Azul's lids and returned 60. By lesson 20, where does Serra Azul stand?
hint: Parts per million: returned over received, times a million.

choices.text: Well inside it, at 0.015%
choices.why: 0.015% is right as a percentage, and it is 150 ppm, which the percentage makes look like nothing.

choices.text: Above it, at 150 ppm
choices.why: Right: 60 ÷ 400,000 × 1,000,000 = 150. That is why customers count in ppm: a contract can set a limit on it.

choices.text: Inside it, at 60 ppm
choices.why: 60 is the count of returns, not a rate per million.

choices.text: It cannot be said without the scrap rate inside the plant
choices.why: Scrap inside the plant and defects at the customer are reported on different scales, and the contract is about the second.

prompt: Two reports of "Tuesday's production" at a plant running three shifts disagree by almost exactly one shift's output. By lesson 20, what is the likeliest reason, and the fix?
hint: The third shift runs from 22:00 to 06:00.

choices.text: Different days for the night shift; a written rule decides
choices.why: Right: a shift crosses midnight and a calendar day does not. Serra Azul writes at the top of every report that a shift belongs to the date it started.

choices.text: One machine's clock is fast; reset the clocks
choices.why: A fast clock moves events by minutes, not a whole shift's output.

choices.text: The operators typed the scrap twice; reconcile with the counter
choices.why: Typed scrap moves a quality figure by a few parts, not a shift's worth of production.

choices.text: One report uses the ERP; drop the machine counters
choices.why: The lesson says to trust the counter for counts; the disagreement here is about dates.
